messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir, a 64-year-old state politician, carried a story that began decades before his polished career, in the dust and chaos of a city under siege. As a young relief worker, he had been negotiating with local militia for the passage of medical supplies. The conversation was tense, conducted through a translator with strangers whose faces he could no longer recall, only the suspicion in their eyes. He remembered the sudden, unnatural silence that fell over the street just moments before the world erupted. The building collapsed around him in a storm of concrete and fire. He survived, but the memory of that day was not a coherent narrative; it was a collection of jagged shards—the smell of burning plastic and insulation, the taste of dust, the high-pitched ringing in his ears.

For years, he managed to keep these fragments at bay by building a life of relentless structure and purpose. Politics provided the perfect vehicle; he threw himself into his work, believing that if he just kept moving, kept achieving, the past couldn't catch up. This strategy of overworking, however, had become a brittle defense. In his office, a debate over a military spending bill would suddenly flood him with a sense of dread, forcing him to excuse himself and bury his head in constituent casework until the feeling subsided. When a trigger like this appeared, his immediate response was to find a distraction, to control the emotion before it could fully form.

These encounters with military topics, or even a tense conversation with an unfamiliar lobbyist, inevitably dredged up pieces of the past. The scent of a backyard barbecue drifting through his window on a summer evening was enough to bring back the smell of the fire, and with it, the same raw terror he felt as he clawed his way out of the rubble. When these memories returned, they were so overwhelming that he felt he had to shut them down immediately. This constant effort to suppress the memories only seemed to make them more fractured and potent when they did break through. His attempts to distract himself and control his emotions left the event unprocessed, ensuring that the next time a memory surfaced, it would be just as terrifying as the last. He has found that because these memory fragments can surface at any time, previously neutral situations have become charged with threat; the memory of the high-pitched ringing that followed the explosion once surfaced while he was alone in his quiet office, and now any deep silence feels menacing to him.

The return of a memory, no matter how fleeting, instantly plunged him into a state of high alert. An image of the collapsed ceiling would leave him feeling profoundly unsafe in his own locked home. He would find himself scanning the quiet suburban street from his window, certain that a threat was lurking just out of sight. This pervasive sense of danger became a constant companion, twisting the world around him. The unusual silence of his empty house at night no longer felt peaceful but menacing, a prelude to disaster, which in turn would often conjure a memory of the silence that preceded the explosion.

This feeling of imminent threat governed his life. It drove him to repeatedly check that his doors and windows were locked, a ritual that provided only momentary relief. The hypervigilance exhausted him, which only amplified his feeling of vulnerability. To escape the belief that something terrible was about to happen, he would retreat further into his work or turn on the television for hours, seeking any distraction to quiet his mind. His focus on external dangers and his attempts to manage his internal state were a closed loop; the more he checked for threats, the more he reinforced the idea that the world was unsafe, and the more he tried to suppress his thoughts, the more exhausted and on edge he became.

His life has slowly constricted. His marriage ended years ago, his ex-wife citing an emotional distance she could never bridge. Now, his career, once his sanctuary, feels like a minefield. He was recently at a town hall when a veteran began to speak, and Amir felt the familiar panic rise. He cut the man off, appearing dismissive and cold, an act that was noted in the local paper. It was this incident, the fear that he was losing control over his public self, that finally brought him to therapy. He fears the fragments in his mind are beginning to define him, and that one day, they will shatter the life he has worked so hard to build.
